title: Typewriters: Mechanical Brilliance
summary: Josh, Chuck and guest Jerry-free co-hosts open with a plug for the Cooperative for Education (CoEd) fall fundraiser, encouraging listeners to donate toward a one million dollar total tied to their Guatemala trips. They then cover the history and mechanics of the typewriter: how manual typewriters work (platen, carriage, type bars, ink ribbon, carriage return bell), early precursors such as Pellegrino Turri's device and the Hansen writing ball, Christopher Latham Sholes and the 1868 patent with Glidden and Soule, the Remington sale and the Sholes and Glidden typewriter, the invention of the shift key, the QWERTY keyboard legend versus the Kyoto research, alternative layouts (Dvorak, Blickensderfer's Die Hard-style bottom-row design), typing classes and typing games, women entering the clerical workforce, typing pools, the Underwood front-stroke visible typewriter, the IBM Selectric, electronic typewriters and early word processors, and a 1994 New York Times prediction about the PC. The episode closes with a listener mail about personalized license plates.

segments.title: Opening banter and CoEd fundraiser plug
segments.summary: The hosts open the episode and plug a CoEd fall fundraiser, encouraging listeners to donate five dollars or so to reach a one million dollar total tied to their Guatemala trip, with a donation URL given.

segments.title: Typewriter impact and early literature
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the typewriter's broad social effects, including creative writing and self publishing, and note Mark Twain's Life on the Mississippi as the first typewritten manuscript submitted. They reflect on their own experience with typewriters and word processors.

segments.title: How a manual typewriter works
segments.summary: The hosts explain manual typewriter parts: the platen, carriage, type bars striking through the ink ribbon, carriage movement, and the carriage return bell and lever.

segments.title: Early precursors to the typewriter
segments.summary: The hosts describe early attempts, including Pellegrino Turri's device for Countess Carolina Fantoni, William Austin Burt's typographer, and the Hansen Writing Ball, which used electromagnets and spread the vowels.

segments.title: Sholes, Glidden and Soule's 1868 patent
segments.summary: Christopher Latham Sholes worked with Carlos Glidden and Samuel Willard Soule to build the 1868 typewriter in Milwaukee, which included the two-spool ribbon design. Their rights were sold to James Densmore in 1872, and Sholes later worked with Matthias Schwalbach on an improved machine.

segments.title: Remington partnership and the shift key
segments.summary: Densmore pitched the typewriter to Remington after the Civil War, leading to the Sholes and Glidden typewriter. Sholes invented the shift key in 1878, and the hosts explain its mechanical origin and why it is called shift rather than caps lock.

segments.title: QWERTY keyboard origins and alternative layouts
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the QWERTY layout, the legend that it was designed to slow typists, and a Kyoto University analysis linking it to Morse code operators. They then cover alternatives: Blickensderfer's bottom-row-heavy layout and the Dvorak Simplified Keyboard from August Dvorak, plus non-Latin keyboards.

segments.title: Learning to type and typing games
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how they learned to type, including hunt-and-peck methods and typing classes and games like Typing Master. They note early typing instruction, possibly from the YWCA of New York in the 1870s.

segments.title: Women in the office and typing pools
segments.summary: The hosts describe how typewriters brought women into clerical work, with women's share of clerical jobs rising from 2.5 percent in 1870 to 52.5 percent in 1930, and how typing pools were used to keep men and women apart in offices. They note the role was tied to single, educated women and that marriage often ended the job.

segments.title: Underwood, IBM Selectric and word processors
segments.summary: The hosts cover the Underwood as the first front-stroke visible typewriter, the IBM Selectric introduced in 1961 with its type ball, electronic typewriters, early word processors such as the Xerox Memory Writer, and a 1990s New York Times prediction about the PC.

segments.title: Listener mail: personalized license plates
segments.summary: A listener named Matt was denied the plate FARTN in Utah and asks for alternatives. The hosts brainstorm options such as TUTING, CRUZN, and DAMTL, and mention Northern Territories license plates from Canada.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners, give the contact email, and note the show is a production of iHeartRadio.
